title: Antiplatelets and anticoagulants in GI bleeding and endoscopy (India, ISG and CSI)
subject: gastroenterology
setting: Emergency department, gastroenterology, endoscopy unit, cardiology liaison
summary: Grade the bleed and the patient's thrombotic risk. Keep aspirin for secondary prevention, stop the second antiplatelet and anticoagulants until haemostasis, avoid platelet transfusion, reverse anticoagulation only for severe bleeding, and restart DAPT within 5 days, DOACs at 3 days and warfarin at 3 to 7 days. Plan endoscopy by urgency and procedural bleeding risk.

sections.title: Grade the bleed and the thrombotic risk
items: GI bleeding: haematemesis, melaena, haematochezia or positive nasogastric aspirate. Classify as upper (within reach of a gastroscope), colonic, or small bowel.

Severe GI bleeding: persistent bleeding in the first 24 hours, need for transfusion, haematocrit fall over 20%, or rebleeding after 24 hours of stability. Use the Glasgow-Blatchford score for upper GI bleeding.
Take a detailed drug history: single or dual antiplatelets, warfarin or acenocoumarol, heparins, DOACs, combinations, and NSAIDs, with the indication for each.
High thrombotic risk on antiplatelets: ACS, any coronary stent, or stroke or TIA within the last 6 months. Otherwise low risk.

High thrombotic risk on anticoagulants: non-valvular AF with CHA2DS2-VASc above 5, metallic mitral valve, prosthetic valve with AF, VTE within 3 months, severe thrombophilia (protein C or S deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome). Otherwise low risk.

sections.title: Acute GI bleeding: resuscitate and adjust drugs
items: Resuscitate first; protect the airway if consciousness is reduced. Transfuse red cells at Hb below 7 g/dL (below 9 g/dL with severe comorbidity) and perform endoscopy within 24 hours.
Aspirin for primary prevention: stop. Aspirin for secondary prevention: continue. Clopidogrel monotherapy for secondary prevention: replace with aspirin.
Dual antiplatelet therapy: continue aspirin, stop the second antiplatelet, and restart it within 5 days of haemostasis.
Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparins, DOACs): interrupt until bleeding is controlled.
Do not give routine platelet transfusion for patients on antiplatelets.

sections.title: Reversal (severe bleeding on anticoagulants)
items: Any anticoagulant: FFP or four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate may be considered; FFP is not routine but can be used for life-threatening bleeding or INR above 3. 4F-PCC is an effective alternative to FFP for warfarin reversal.
Warfarin: vitamin K 2 to 5 mg orally or IV reverses anticoagulation (INR 1.3 or below) over 24 to 48 hours; it does not give rapid haemostasis.
DOAC taken within 2 to 4 hours: consider a single dose of activated charcoal 50 g.
Idarucizumab (dabigatran) and andexanet alfa (factor Xa inhibitors) can be used in selected life-threatening bleeds; cost and availability limit routine use.
Endoscopic haemostasis: standard techniques; mechanical methods (clips) are preferred over thermal methods in anticoagulated patients.

sections.title: Restarting after haemostasis
items: DAPT: restart within 5 days of bleeding control, preferably aspirin plus clopidogrel; shorten DAPT to 6 months and add a daily PPI.
Aspirin monotherapy that was interrupted: restart as soon as possible with a PPI.
Warfarin: restart after 3 days (high thrombotic risk) to 7 days (low risk); in high-risk patients overlap LMWH until INR is therapeutic; keep strict INR control.
DOAC: restart 3 days after haemostasis. Options: switch to warfarin with strict INR control, or from dabigatran or rivaroxaban to apixaban, which has a lower bleeding risk.
Resuming anticoagulation lowers thromboembolism and mortality without clearly increasing rebleeding: do not stop it permanently without a strong reason.

sections.title: Planned endoscopy for non-bleeding indications
items: Classify urgency: urgent within 24 hours (for example CBD stenting in cholangitis), semi-urgent within 2 to 7 days (CBD stone removal), elective deferrable for weeks to months (POEM).

Low bleeding risk (muscularis mucosae not breached): diagnostic gastroscopy or colonoscopy with or without biopsy, ERCP without sphincterotomy, biliary or pancreatic stenting, diagnostic EUS, enteroscopy. Continue single or dual antiplatelets; omit the DOAC on the day of the procedure; for warfarin, check the INR is within the therapeutic range.

High bleeding risk (muscularis mucosae breached): polypectomy, EMR, ESD, sphincterotomy, POEM, stricture dilatation, stenting, PEG, EUS-guided sampling or drainage, variceal ligation or sclerotherapy, glue injection, necrosectomy, APC.
High-risk procedure on DAPT: defer until the minimum DAPT period is complete; if not possible, continue aspirin, stop the second drug 7 days before and restart 1 to 2 days after.
High-risk procedure on aspirin alone: continue aspirin. On a DOAC: stop 3 days before and restart 2 to 3 days after (consider creatinine clearance).

High-risk procedure on warfarin: stop 5 days before and confirm INR below 1.5; restart after the procedure. High thrombotic risk: switch to LMWH 5 days before, omit LMWH on the procedure day, then overlap LMWH with warfarin until INR is therapeutic.
Urgent life-saving endoscopy can proceed regardless of antithrombotics, but avoid cutting (for example sphincterotomy) where possible.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Stopping aspirin in a patient with a recent stent or ACS, raising the risk of stent thrombosis.
Transfusing platelets for antiplatelet-associated bleeding.
Leaving anticoagulants stopped indefinitely after a controlled bleed.
Continuing primary-prevention aspirin after a GI bleed.
Making drug changes without discussing high thrombotic risk patients with the cardiologist or neurologist.

drugs.name: Vitamin K (phytomenadione)
drugs.notes: Warfarin reversal over 24 to 48 hours; not for rapid haemostasis.

drugs.name: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate or FFP
drugs.dose: Consider for severe bleeding on any anticoagulant (FFP especially if INR above 3)
drugs.notes: The position statement does not specify doses; dose per product and INR.

drugs.name: Activated charcoal
drugs.notes: If a DOAC was taken within 2 to 4 hours.

drugs.name: Proton pump inhibitor
drugs.dose: Once daily with resumed aspirin or DAPT
